one_liner: C++20 SIMD XML parser with a flat 32-byte-node DOM; 1.6-3.3x pugixml's read-only parse throughput on synthetic XML.
what_it_does: A C++20 XML library with Python bindings. It offers several parsers: fast_dom_parse (a read-only flat 'FastDom' of index-linked 32-byte nodes), dom_parse (a pointer-linked XmlDocument), SAX, pull (StAX-style) and chunked streaming. It also ships a partial XPath 1.0 engine, a writer/DomBuilder and internal-DTD validation. It is not a drop-in for pugixml: you navigate by FastNode (dom.first_child(n), dom.attr(n, "id")), values are string_views into your buffer with no NUL terminator, and FastDom has no API for changing the tree.
how_it_is_fast: It makes a single pass over the input. AVX2 32-byte compare+movemask+ctz scans (_mm256_cmpeq_epi8/_mm256_movemask_epi8) jump to the next '<', closing quote or comment/CDATA end, and names are read with a scalar lookup table. Nodes are 32-byte structs written in order into one malloc'd array, which starts at len/35 nodes and doubles with realloc. They are linked by uint32 indices, not pointers, and names and attribute values stay as pointers or offsets into the input (zero-copy). The benchmarked FDOM_FASTEST mode also skips building text nodes. The parser never matches end-tag names or reports errors, so it does less work than pugixml. The author puts the 64 MB+ gap over RapidXML down to RapidXML's per-node allocation versus this one flat array.
when_to_use: Read-only extraction of element structure and attributes (not text) from trusted, well-formed UTF-8 XML, which is exactly the FDOM_FASTEST shape that was benchmarked
Large documents (64-128 MB) on x86-64 with AVX2, where the README shows 1.5-1.8x over RapidXML and 1.85-2.6x over pugixml
Replacing a pugixml load_buffer + walk used only for reading, when you can adopt an index-based API with string_view results and keep the input buffer alive
Python batch jobs over trusted XML that need more than lxml's roughly 90-106 MB/s (README reports 527-575 MB/s), provided raw, entity-undecoded text is acceptable
Open-source projects already under AGPL-3.0-or-later, or teams willing to buy the commercial license
when_not_to_use: Untrusted or possibly malformed input: neither fast_dom_parse nor dom_parse checks that end tags match or reports parse errors. The project's own W3C run shows 928 of 1383 not-wf cases wrongly accepted (SAX path)
Closed-source products or SaaS without a paid license: AGPL-3.0 §13 network-use copyleft, whereas pugixml (MIT) and RapidXML are permissive
Files of 64 KB-16 MB where you already use RapidXML: Parshred's own table shows parity within ~5% there, and RapidXML is header-only
Needs beyond read-only DOM: editing the tree in place, pugixml's full XPath 1.0 (ancestor/preceding axes and variables are missing), namespace-aware DOM/XPath, or UTF-16/Latin-1 input (UTF-8 only)

Workloads that need production maturity: single author, 0 stars, and all code landed 2026-07-11 to 07-29 with no commits since. The weekly fuzz job has failed twice in fuzz_xpath (out-of-memory in xpath::eval_step and UBSan float-to-integer overflow in xpath.hpp)

integration.dependencies: none at runtime (vcpkg.json lists none); GoogleTest and Google Benchmark are fetched only for tests/benchmarks; pybind11 only for the Python module
integration.min_toolchain: C++20; README: GCC 12+, Clang 15+, MSVC 2022+; CMake 3.20+ (CI builds GCC 13, Clang 17, AppleClang on macos-14, MSVC 2022)
integration.platforms: x86-64 (README says SSE4.2 minimum, but FastDOM's SIMD needs your own TU compiled with -mavx2) and aarch64 (NEON helpers exist but are not called by the FastDOM/SAX paths checked, so scalar there); Linux, macOS, Windows
integration.thread_safety: not documented. fast_dom_parse keeps its state on the stack and in the returned FastDom, so separate parses on separate threads look independent; MmapReader is documented as not thread-safe

gotchas: The parsers lose data silently. fast_dom_parse drops CDATA sections entirely and leaves entities undecoded unless you pass FDOM_NORMALIZE. value_len is a uint16, so values over 65535 bytes are truncated. Nesting beyond 255 levels (64 for dom_parse) quietly corrupts the tree, even though conformance.md claims dom_parse throws at depth 512. The Python binding uses fast_dom_parse<0>, so Python users hit the CDATA and entity behaviour too.

fast_dom_parse chooses SIMD at compile time: simd_utils.hpp is gated on #ifdef __AVX2__, so a TU built without -mavx2/-march gets scalar byte loops. The CPUID runtime dispatch covers only the simd_scan backends, and the PyPI binding module is built with plain -O3.

FastDom stores raw pointers and 32-bit offsets into the caller's buffer, so the buffer must outlive the DOM. Offsets and indices are uint32, which implies a 4 GiB input limit (not documented). Parent lookup (XPath '..') scans the whole node array, O(n).

parallel_fast_dom_parse splits only where nesting depth returns to 0, so a normal single-root document falls back to serial. The README's FetchContent snippet pins v0.1.0, but the latest tag is v0.1.6. Some docs are stale: performance.md has older numbers, and the migration guide describes an 80-byte XmlNode with a parent pointer, but the code has a 64-byte node with no parent.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over RapidXml when documents are 64 MB or larger (1.5-1.8x in its own table) or when you want XPath and Python bindings, and AGPL or a commercial license is acceptable; below 16 MB, RapidXml is at parity, header-only and permissively licensed. Against libsimdxml (about 1.2-1.25x over pugixml on an old i7) it claims a bigger pugixml margin, but on different hardware and a synthetic workload. Use SpeedyXml instead for measured real-world streaming.
verified_claims_summary: Setup: generated <item id name status>text</item> records at 64 KB-128 MB, single thread, Ryzen 5 7640U, GCC 16.1 -O3 -mavx2. fast_dom_parse<FDOM_FASTEST>, which builds no text nodes, ran at 1317-2722 MB/s against pugixml 1.14 load_buffer(parse_minimal) at 641-1585 MB/s, a 1.6x-3.3x gap. It matched RapidXML 1.13 parse_fastest within ~5% up to 16 MB and was 1.5-1.8x faster at 64-128 MB. These are first-party numbers, and pugixml copies the buffer and still builds PCDATA nodes, so the pugixml ratio overstates a same-work comparison.
status_note: Young single-author project (created 2026-07-11, last commit 2026-07-29 at v0.1.6, also on PyPI, 0 stars, no issues filed). It is usable under AGPL-3.0-or-later or a paid commercial license, not permissively.
